answer.title: The voice on the line
answer.text:
You answer before the second ring.

For a moment all you hear is someone breathing too close to a microphone. You are about to ask who it is when the person outside knocks. The breath on the line catches at exactly the same time as yours.

You don't say your name. You learned that much from a school assembly about scams, though the person giving the assembly did not discuss visitors wearing your face.

The voice says, ‘Sam?’

You put the phone on the counter. You want both hands free. You don't know what you expect to do with them.

silence.title: The black screen
silence.text:
You hold the power button until the screen goes black. For two seconds the flat is quiet.

Then the phone rings again. The screen stays dark.

You put it on the counter and step away. This feels like the sort of thing that should solve a problem if you do it decisively enough. It doesn't.

The third knock comes from the door.

A voice from the black phone says, ‘Sam? Please. I know you can hear it.’

You recognise the voice, and that is worse than not recognising it.

Eventually you touch the screen. It lights up with the same call still waiting, as though the phone has simply refused to take part in your decision. You answer without putting it to your ear.

include.title: An invitation
include.text:
‘I'm going to need help,’ you tell Imani. ‘I don't know what kind yet.’

She looks towards the road. ‘Then don't tell me I have to. Ask.’

You try again. ‘Will you come?’

‘Yes.’ She checks the map on her phone. ‘And I'm telling my dad where we are.’

Miso steps around a puddle. ‘Sensible.’

‘You can carry your own phone when you grow thumbs,’ she tells him.

He looks offended. You leave them to establish their own relationship.

dismiss.title: Keeping up
dismiss.text:
‘Just keep up,’ you say. ‘I'll explain when I can.’

Imani stops.

You get three steps farther before noticing. When you turn, she is still standing by the bins.

‘I'm not your employee,’ she says.

‘I didn't mean—’

‘Then use different words.’

You look at the map on your phone. You don't know whether the next street is the safe one. She doesn't either. That is not a reason to pretend she agreed to be instructed.

‘Will you come to the annex?’ you ask.

She considers it. ‘Your aunt asked me to check on you. I'm doing that. We'll see after.’

She walks beside you, leaving more space than before.

fare-negotiate.title: A limited fare
fare-negotiate.text:
‘Tell me what the transfer gives you before I pay,’ you say.

The driver's hand remains open. ‘A record that you entered this road willingly. No claim on your return. No permission to speak for you.’

‘And you keep what I say?’

‘Only the account needed for the crossing.’

You think about it, then tell him you left a kitchen where your mother's things have begun to look like somebody else's clutter. You don't give him every memory attached to that sentence.

He stamps the transfer and gives it to you. ‘Defined terms,’ he says. ‘A useful habit.’

Imani puts her fare away. ‘We're keeping that habit.’

You sit down together. Miso climbs out of your collar, dislodging a considerable amount of fur onto your coat.

fare-lie.title: A pretty answer
fare-lie.text:
‘Nothing,’ you say. ‘I haven't left anything.’

In the window, your reflection smiles. You haven't moved your mouth.

The driver closes his hand. ‘Then I cannot issue the transfer.’

The doors remain open. Beyond them, the staircase is visible. You can get there, but it will not count as a witnessed crossing.

You feel a moment of triumph, followed by the uncomfortable recognition that you have won nothing except permission to leave without the thing you need.

Imani steps down first. She does not look at you until both feet are on the concrete.

‘Was that worth it?’

‘I don't know yet.’

‘Next time, work that out before.’

Miso follows, saying nothing at all.

fare-force.title: The barrier
fare-force.text:
You try to push past the driver's arm.

You do not get far. The space beyond the fare reader lengthens while your feet stay where they are. Your elbow strikes the rail hard enough to make your fingers numb.

The driver has not moved.

‘You may refuse passage,’ he says. ‘You may not turn everyone else's road into your entrance.’

Imani takes your good arm and pulls you back. You let her. The shame comes before the pain, which is an unpleasant order for either feeling.

At the next ordinary landing, the doors open. No transfer. No blessing. A way out which remains a way out because he said it would.

On the concrete, you unwrap the dressing at your elbow and see fresh blood. Imani has stopped asking whether it hurts.

fare-refuse.title: The open door
fare-refuse.text:
‘I don't want to give you that,’ you say.

The driver inclines his head. ‘Then use the exit.’

You expected an argument. Getting none makes you hesitate.

Imani steps down beside you. Miso follows. The streetcar remains until you are clear of the doors, then moves away across the river.

‘We still reach the exchange room?’ you ask.

‘We walk farther,’ Miso says. ‘Not every refusal ends the road.’

The steps are steep and your boots are wet. You spend the climb thinking about the question you chose not to answer. You don't decide whether you should have answered it. You are glad the decision was allowed to remain yours.

share.title: The copied numbers
share.text:
You show Imani the back of the photograph before putting the notebook away.

‘Those were under Eva's name,’ you say. ‘I copied the crossed-out one too.’

She takes a picture of your page, discovers the photograph comes out blank, and writes the numbers into her own notebook instead.

‘Two copies,’ she says. ‘If one of us drops something off another roof.’

‘We haven't been on a roof.’

‘Give it time.’

You laugh. When the fear returns, you don't have to carry the information alone with it.

withhold.title: The useful thing
withhold.text:
You close the notebook before Imani can see the back of the photograph.

‘Anything else he gave you?’ she asks.

‘No.’

The word comes easily. You tell yourself you are checking the numbers before worrying anyone. You tell yourself you will share them when they make sense.

Imani watches you put the notebook away.

‘Okay,’ she says.

You had wanted the lie to end the question. It does. That is not as reassuring as you expected.

submit.title: Submitted for correction
submit.text:
You slide the evidence across the desk.

Thoth gives you a receipt with a clear list of what he is retaining. You check the recorder's serial number, though you have never cared about a serial number in your life. Julian checks it too.

‘Copies remain yours,’ Thoth says. ‘The correction will show both the false entry and the evidence against it.’

You nod. You are not buying the disappearance of a bad fact. You are making it possible for someone else to see what happened.

steal.title: The book that closes
steal.text:
You grab the open book.

It shuts before you can lift it. Your sleeve is caught between the covers. The third pen stops above the page, perfectly still.

Thoth looks at your hand.

‘You came to challenge a stolen authority.’

You let go. The sleeve comes free with a neat tear along the seam.

Julian has gone pale. Imani steps back from the desk. You cannot think of an answer that makes the last five seconds look better.

Thoth copies the public route reference onto a card and puts it beyond your reach. ‘You may take the address. You may not use my witness seal.’

You take the card only after he nods. The walk to the stairs feels very long.

archive-refuse.title: The evidence you keep
archive-refuse.text:
‘I'm keeping the recorder,’ you say.

Thoth withdraws the evidence form. ‘Then I cannot certify the correction.’

‘Can you give us the address?’

He considers the reference number, then writes a public routing entry on a card. ‘A destination. Not proof of your authority to change what happens there.’

You take it. Your mother's voice remains in your pocket. The witness receipt stays on his desk.

Julian does not tell you that you chose badly. He asks you to put the difference in the notebook so nobody later assumes you have something you don't.

save-julian.title: The sleeve in your hand
save-julian.text:
You grab Julian's sleeve and pull.

He comes away from the panel with a sharp cry. His hand has gone grey to the wrist. You get his good arm over your shoulder and take his weight before your injured elbow can object.

Behind him, the spare connector remains in the socket. You see it. You know it might have helped. You keep moving.

Julian tries to say your name. You tell him to save the breath until he is through the door.

Imani takes his other side. Together you get him over the threshold.

take-connector.title: One more piece
take-connector.text:
You reach for the spare connector.

The metal is hot enough to burn through your glove. You pull it free and fall against the panel. Behind you, Imani swears and hauls Julian away from the closing contact.

‘Sam!’

You turn. His injured hand hangs at a wrong, stiff angle. She has his good arm over her shoulder, carrying a weight you chose not to reach first.

You help them through the door with the connector burning in your pocket. It may be useful. It doesn't make Imani meet your eyes.

Julian says, ‘You got it, then,’ in a voice you cannot read.

rink-stay.title: The full session
rink-stay.text:
You put the phone away.

For the rest of the session you watch the puck closely enough to lose it twice. You don't understand every decision Imani makes, but you begin to recognise when she's pleased with one.

When she looks towards the benches again, you are still there.

The archive message can wait until the whistle. You don't pretend waiting was easy. It matters that you chose it anyway.

rink-leave.title: The spare hour
rink-leave.text:
You show Imani's dad the message and say you need to go. He nods, distracted by a shot at the far end of the rink.

Outside, you call Leila before going to the flat. She meets you there. Together you find the manual before Imani's session finishes. It is a useful hour. You keep telling yourself that while looking at your phone.

Imani's message arrives at eleven thirty: Went looking for you. Dad said you had another thing.

You start an explanation, delete half of it and send the plain version: I left to find the manual. Should've told you myself.

Her reply comes several minutes later. Yes.

When she joins you at the flat, she asks to read the diagram before agreeing to the next part of the plan.

wren-ask.title: A question she can answer
wren-ask.text:
‘You don't have to keep us here,’ you tell the girl. ‘What happens if we leave?’

She looks at the door. ‘He asks why I let you.’

‘You can say we asked you.’

‘That won't be enough.’

You don't tell her it will. Instead you ask whether she wants to come as far as the window and see the roof herself.

She moves aside. Only a little. Enough to let Imani reach the catch without pushing past her.

‘Just looking,’ she says.

‘Just looking,’ you agree.

wren-deceive.title: A false instruction
wren-deceive.text:
‘Voss said to let us take the reader,’ you say. ‘It's part of the test.’

The girl's face brightens with relief. Then it tightens.

‘He would have told me.’

You point towards the door. ‘Ask him.’

She turns for long enough that Imani can reach the window. You have bought a few seconds by making another person doubt what she was told.

When the girl turns back, she knows. You can see it before she speaks.

‘You do that too,’ she says.

The cable nearest your boot coils tightly enough to crack the floor tile.

wren-attack.title: The swing
wren-attack.text:
You swing the torch towards her hand, trying to knock the cable away.

It goes through her wrist. The force of your own movement pulls you off balance. You hit the cupboard hard with your injured elbow.

The girl looks down at the place you tried to strike. Her face becomes your mother's for one terrible second.

‘Don't,’ Imani says. You aren't sure which of you she means.

You get up. The torch has broken against the wood. The girl steps back from you, opening a path without offering trust.

Outside the door, Voss begins turning the handle.

wren-refuse.title: No bargain
wren-refuse.text:
‘We're taking the reader,’ you say. ‘I'm not making a deal about my mother.’

The girl watches you. ‘I wasn't asking for her.’

You look at the cable in her hand and realise you heard a threat before she made one.

‘Then let us leave.’

She steps away from the window. ‘You can. I don't have to like it.’

Imani opens the catch. Cold air moves through the room. You keep watching the girl's face, expecting another borrowed one. It stays her own unfinished shape.

For once, nobody makes the refusal mean more than it does.

gate-negotiate.title: A road for everyone
gate-negotiate.text:
You offer the witness papers with your hands open.

‘Passage for those who choose it. Return for the same people, if they choose to leave. No replacement required.’

Wepwawet examines the receiving record. He looks at Wren, not at you.

‘Your choice?’

‘Mine,’ she says.

The standard lifts. The stone doors part far enough for the equipment bag.

‘The road is open,’ he says. ‘Keep the terms you named.’

You step through without trying to take a piece of the opening with you.

gate-name.title: The name in the margin
gate-name.text:
‘Wepwawet,’ you say, carefully. ‘Opener of the Ways. I ask for a road, not control of it.’

His shadow moves before he does. For a moment the jackal on the standard seems larger than the room.

‘You know which work you are asking for.’

You show him the page in Nadia's notebook. He reads the little correction beside the sketch.

‘She learned.’

‘So are we.’

He turns the standard aside. The gap widens. Knowledge has not made him yours to command; it has let you make a request he can recognise.

Wren goes through beside you, holding her card in one hand.

gate-force.title: The way you cannot own
gate-force.text:
You push towards the opening.

The standard strikes the floor. The sound knocks the breath from your lungs. You land on your knees, skin burning where the stone scrapes through your jeans.

Wepwawet has not struck you. He has stopped the road moving with you on it. The distinction does not improve the pain.

Imani puts the equipment bag down before helping you stand.

‘You have a route back,’ the god says. ‘Take it if you will not ask for passage.’

You look at the blood on your knee, then at the person holding the door.

‘Passage,’ you say. The word is difficult to get out. ‘For everyone who chooses it.’

He waits until you have named the return terms too. Only then does the opening widen.

gate-refuse.title: The road above
gate-refuse.text:
You look through the opening towards the lower station. Then at the equipment bag. Then at the line of water beside the stairs.

‘I can't promise the conditions,’ you say. ‘We turn back.’

Voss starts to object. Leila stops him before the first full sentence.

Wepwawet moves the standard away from the upper stair. No punishment. No offer made crueler by being withdrawn.

The climb back is slow. At the top, Dennis sees your faces and reaches for the bell case.

Nadia is still on the other side. Breaking the outer line may release her through the old return, but there is no one beside her to guide the way. You have accepted that uncertainty by turning around.

Leila opens the controlled voice channel so Nadia can hear the plan. You wait for her answer before anyone touches the bell.
